notes.carers_allowance_earnings_taper: Our static estimate is about 60% of the official costing in both compared years: £24 million against £40 million in 2030-31, and £48 million against £80 million in 2031-32. The official figure, the OBR's £38 million and £79 million before the Treasury rounds them, includes £5 million and £10 million of extra block grant for Scotland, where Carer's Allowance is devolved; the rest, £33 million and £69 million, is Carer's Allowance and Universal Credit spending, with no line for income tax (OBR policy Table 1.1). Before the income tax on the higher allowance (£15 million and £32 million), which our net cost subtracts, ours is £39 million and £79 million, about a sixth more than that spending. The official figure also includes a labour-supply response, which ours does not, and the model does not count the income tax collected on the allowance through PAYE against Universal Credit earnings, which makes its Universal Credit saving larger.
notes.domestic_electricity_zero_vat: Our cost is £85m (11%) above the official costing in 2026-27 and £48m (16%) above it in 2027-28. The official costing also covers charities, residential care and some businesses, and it counts households switching from gas to electricity; both make the official figure larger, so neither explains the gap. Ours starts from DESNZ's domestic electricity volumes at average prices paid, grown with CPI. The official costing starts from ONS consumer spending, which is 10% to 12% lower; at that level our cost would be within about 4% of the official figure in both years.
notes.fuel_duty_rise_deferral: Our cost is £274 million below the official costing in 2026-27 (£301 million against £575 million) and £259 million below in 2027-28 (£521 million against £780 million); from 2028-29 both are zero. Most of the gap is coverage: we count only the petrol and diesel that households buy, about £13 billion of the £24 billion of fuel duty the OBR forecasts for 2026-27, while the official costing covers all taxable fuel, including fuel that businesses buy, and scaled to the OBR's fuel duty receipts our fuel duty cost would be about £450 million in 2026-27 and £760 million in 2027-28. VAT and behaviour narrow the gap rather than explain it (ours includes £50 million and £87 million of VAT on the lower pump price, which the official fuel duty figure leaves out, and the official costing's demand response makes its cost smaller). The rest of the 2026-27 gap fits the official costing assuming the full 5p returns on 1 January 2027 (about £555 million on 45 billion litres), where the law brings it back as 3p and then 2p from 1 March (about £410 million).
notes.household_energy_payment_2026: Our £1,969 million in 2026-27 is 25% below the official £2,625 million, because the official figure also covers two things we don't model: the devolved governments' share of the funding (about £425 million, our estimate using the Barnett formula) and £100 million for councils in England to target the households hit hardest. Without them, about £2,100 million remains for the £100 payments in England, and our estimate is 94% of that; the Budget doesn't itemise the remaining £130 million or so. Both estimates are zero in every later year.
notes.property_income_rates_up: The official costing puts the tax later than the year it's owed: the OBR adds almost no Self Assessment receipts from the savings and property rate rises in 2027-28 and £1.0bn in 2028-29, so those two years aren't comparable with our tax-year figures. From 2029-30 we're within 1.5% of the Treasury's costing (Table 6.1) every year, +£429m against +£435m in 2029-30 (the OBR's own table has £400m). The official costing takes off about £0.1bn a year for landlords incorporating and lower compliance, which ours leaves out, so before behaviour ours is about £0.1bn a year lower.
notes.state_pension_income_tax_protection: The official costing counts no benefit savings: its income tax is £44m, £83m and £144m (OBR detailed table 1.1). Ours is £42m, £112m and £193m: about 5% lower in 2027-28 and 35% and 34% higher in 2028-29 and 2029-30. More pensioners gain in our data (about 670,000 in 2027-28, against the Treasury's 500,000). After Pension Credit, Housing Benefit and Council Tax Reduction take back part of it, our net cost is £30m, £83m and £144m. For 2028-29 and 2029-30 we set the allowance at £182 and £250 a year, from the October 2026 forecast of the State Pension.
notes.trading_allowance_raise: From 2028-29 our estimate is £46m to £107m a year below the Treasury's (28% to 47%), with the largest gap in 2028-29. The Treasury's costing includes people switching from actual expenses to the larger allowance, which we don't model. Without gross receipts in the survey data, we give traders with profits above £3,000 nothing from the change and give miscellaneous income no allowance at all, while for some profits between £1,000 and £3,000 we overstate the gain, because we leave them unrelieved under the current £1,000 allowance.

statement: Gaps come from timing, coverage, behaviour and scope.

caveats.timing: Our figures are by tax year. The official costings are on a National Accounts basis, in which tax paid through Self Assessment can fall in a later year: a change in it, such as the trading allowance, can appear about a year later in them than in ours.
